cutoff_note: frozen / neutralised: the frozen 5:1 cut-off (chosen on the frozen model's training OOF); nodemo: the same cost rule (tune_threshold(..., 'cost'), grid 0.05-0.95 step 0.01) on its own training OOF
cutoff_source: results/<slug>.json at_tuned_cost.threshold (chosen by tune_threshold(y_train, p_oof, 'cost') on the training OOF; equals frozen_manifest.json thresholds_chosen_on_training_oof.cost and is re-derived here)

variants.xgb_frozen / logit_frozen: frozen training OOF probabilities, read from results/<slug>_p_oof.npy
variants.xgb_neutralised / logit_neutralised: frozen settings refitted per fold in memory (reproduces the frozen OOF vector); validation clients scored with SEX = female, AGE = 34, MARRIAGE = single, EDUCATION = university -> removes the direct use of the attributes
variants.xgb_nodemo / logit_nodemo: same settings refitted per fold on the 25 non-demographic predictors (no SEX, AGE, MARRIAGE, EDUCATION)

plain_notes: Base rates differ before any model is involved: in the training rows men default at 24.5% and women at 20.6% (ratio 1.19); married clients 23.7% vs single 20.8%; clients aged 50+ 25.0% vs 30-39 20.5%.

The frozen XGBoost is calibrated in the large within every group of 1,000 or more clients (|mean PD - observed rate| at most 0.50 percentage points) and flags men 1.18 times as often as women (54.7% vs 46.5%), close to the default-rate ratio of 1.19. A score calibrated within groups usually flags more of a higher-risk group, and here it also flags more of that group's non-defaulters: FPR 45.7% for men vs 38.2% for women. A flag ratio that matches the base rates does not mean the attributes are unused: scoring every client with the reference values narrows the XGBoost sex ratio to 1.09 and the married/single ratio to 0.99, so part of the XGBoost gap is direct use of SEX and MARRIAGE and part comes through the other predictors. With different base rates, equal calibration, equal flag rates and equal error rates cannot all hold at once (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan 2017; Chouldechova 2017).

The plain logit widens the gaps beyond the base rates: it flags men 1.36 times as often as women (FPR ratio 1.44) and married clients 1.33 times as often as single ones, although it is calibrated within these groups. Its SEX and MARRIAGE coefficients shift every member's log-odds by the same amount, and the logit's PDs are packed more tightly around the cut-off (0.15): 5.1% of clients per 0.01 of PD near it, against 3.5% for XGBoost (both medians are close to the cut-off: logit 0.142, XGBoost 0.149), so the same shift moves more clients across it. Neutralising the attributes brings the sex ratio to 1.08 and the marital ratio to 1.00: most of the logit's excess gap is direct use of the attribute.

Refitting without SEX, AGE, MARRIAGE and EDUCATION costs little ranking power: XGBoost CV AUC -0.0021 (95% corrected t CI -0.0041 to -0.0002; 0/5 folds positive), AP -0.0011 (95% corrected t CI -0.0074 to +0.0051; 3/5 folds positive); logit AUC -0.0037 (95% corrected t CI -0.0079 to +0.0004; 0/5 folds positive). It narrows the sex gap (XGBoost flag ratio 1.18 -> 1.10) and removes the marital gap (1.12 -> 0.99), but the price is within-group calibration: the model now under-predicts men by 1.1 and over-predicts women by 0.7 percentage points.

Removing an attribute does not always narrow a gap. Clients under 30 are flagged more often without AGE (ratio to 30-39 1.11 -> 1.17; FPR 42.2% -> 45.5%) and become over-predicted by 0.9 points. Their credit limits are low (median 90,000 vs 170,000 NT$), and at the same limit quintile they default less often than older clients (5 of 5 limit quintiles, see mechanism_checks), so once AGE is gone the low limit is read as more risk than it carries for them. The small 'others/unknown' education bucket (n = 343, default rate 6.7%) goes from 10.8% flagged to 35.9%; this bucket pools 'others', 'unknown' and the undocumented code 0, so its numbers say more about how education was recorded than about a real group of people.

Removing the columns does not remove proxies. From the 25 remaining predictors alone, out-of-fold AUC for recovering the attribute is 0.60 for sex, 0.65 for age under 30, 0.56 for single, 0.69 for graduate school (R^2 for age in years 0.037); LIMIT_BAL is the leading proxy in every case. The proxies are weak to moderate here, but they are why a demographics-free score still differs by group, and why 'fairness through unawareness' is not by itself a fairness guarantee.

What a review in the style of the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, which lists creditworthiness assessment and credit scoring of natural persons as high-risk in Annex III point 5(b)) or of the MAS FEAT principles would ask for: a stated justification for each personal attribute used (FEAT fairness principle on personal attributes); data-governance evidence that possible biases were examined and mitigated (AI Act Article 10); a risk-management record and technical documentation that state the fairness criterion chosen, the reference groups and the trade-offs accepted, with group-level metrics like these (Articles 9 and 11; the MAS Veritas fairness assessment methodology asks for the same steps); human oversight of declines (Article 14); monitoring of the group metrics after deployment (Article 72); and, for the deploying lender, a fundamental-rights impact assessment (Article 27) and an explanation route for declined applicants (Article 86). Article numbers should be checked against the Official Journal text before citing. This table is diagnostic evidence for such a review, not a legal assessment: the data are Taiwanese card clients from 2005 and no regulation is claimed to apply to them, nor is any model here claimed to be compliant or non-compliant.
